metadata.title: AI Use Cases | Sébastien Donné | TKoidra
metadata.description: Functional AI demonstrators, live and testable — from framing to production, illustrated by use cases in insurance, real estate, and compliance.

appLink.label: Open the application
appLink.coldStartNote: ⏳ Slower first load: to keep costs down, the demo goes to sleep when no one is using it. On first access, the server restarts; after that, it responds normally.

assurconseil.title: AssurConseil RAG
assurconseil.description: Agentic RAG assistant for insurance contract interpretation, with a Claude / Mistral comparison in document mode.
assurconseil.demonstrates: Industrialising a RAG: evaluation before production, cost guardrails, proven European inference, progressive deployment.
assurconseil.challenge: Insurance advisors must navigate dozens of pages of general terms to answer client questions accurately, under regulatory duty-to-advise obligations — a misread clause or wrongly cited guarantee exposes the insurer to liability.
assurconseil.solution: An agentic RAG assistant that routes each question to the most suitable pattern (ReAct for direct lookups, Plan-and-Execute for multi-part questions), with mandatory source citation and explicit refusal to answer when no supporting document exists — a demo built on fictional contracts and a fictional company (ARESIA Assurances), illustrating an agentic architecture for regulated advisory use cases. In document mode, the same question is sent in parallel to Claude and Mistral Large 3 (Mistral inference run in the EU): answers side by side, with latency, tokens and cost.

features.title: Adaptive ReAct / Plan-and-Execute Routing
features.description: A router detects question complexity and switches between direct retrieval (ReAct) and sub-question decomposition (Plan-and-Execute).

features.title: Anti-Hallucination Guardrail
features.description: Mandatory citation of source articles; an explicit "not found" response rather than a fabricated answer when information is absent from the documents.

features.title: Full Reasoning Traceability
features.description: Every graph step (router, retrieve, evaluate, synthesize) is logged in an inspectable trace_log, from question to final answer.

features.title: Your Contract, Two Engines
features.description: Upload a contract: temporary in-memory index, separate from the corpus. The same question goes in parallel to Claude and Mistral Large 3 (EU inference); answers side by side with latency, tokens and estimated cost.

image.alt: Screenshot of the Claude / Mistral Large 3 comparison on AssurConseil RAG: an answer to a question about a provident contract's deductibles, with cited sources, latency, tokens and cost shown for each engine.

fraud.title: Fraud Agent
fraud.description: Pre-assessment agent for P&C insurance claims: business rules set the routing, a Claude agent proposes, a claims handler decides.
fraud.demonstrates: Designing a bounded agent for a regulated business: what the code decides, what the agent proposes, what the human approves, with measured cost and latency.
fraud.tag: Agentic AI · Human in the Loop
fraud.challenge: In a claims department, most cases are simple, but those that call for an investigation or a recovery claim against a liable third party require cross-checking several documents. Handing this work to AI raises three questions: who decides the routing, what happens when the model gets it wrong, and what does it cost?
fraud.solution: On fictional claims, business rules compute a score out of 50 and set the routing (straight-through processing, investigation, fraud-unit alert). The agent cannot change it. A Claude agent is called only when useful, when the case is suspicious or a police report is provided. It picks its tools, returns a structured proposal, then stops: a claims handler approves or rejects it with a reason, before the agent drafts a letter that is never actually sent. Thresholds are demonstration choices, not calibrated on real data.

features.title: Rules first, AI when useful
features.description: Score and routing come from deterministic rules. A clean case without a police report triggers no AI call.

features.title: An agent that picks its tools
features.description: Depending on the case, the agent checks the repair shop's history or computes the recovery amount. Every step shows in a log (tool, input, output, duration), and amounts are recomputed by the code.

features.title: Mandatory human approval
features.description: The handler approves, or rejects with a reason. A recovery letter draft and a D+5 / D+15 / D+30 plan follow, marked "never actually sent".

metrics: 15 live analyses per day, then a labelled replay (measured on 01/10/2026)

image.alt: Screenshot of an analysis on Fraud Agent: rules score of 0 out of 50, straight-through routing, the agent's step-by-step run and the start of its proposal, on a fictional claim.

methodBridge.label: Same method as AssurConseil RAG: cut the risks before adding features, measure before announcing a figure, rehearse in preview before going to production.

agap.title: AGAP
agap.description: AI-arbitrated project portfolio prioritization, free of Business/IT bias.
agap.demonstrates: Tooling a portfolio decision: surfacing Business/IT gaps and arbitrating through scenarios, with tracked justifications.
agap.challenge: A Portfolio Director arbitrates dozens of projects every year based on structurally biased Business and IT declarations: Business overstates business impact, IT overstates effort and technical risk to protect itself. Without a mediation mechanism, final arbitration becomes a political power struggle rather than an objective decision.
agap.solution: A governance application that has a Claude agent separately challenge each Business and IT declaration, computes a confidence index and an adjusted attractiveness score, then visualizes perception conflicts before final arbitration — a demo built on a fictional 6-project portfolio, illustrating neutral AI mediation between two parties with diverging interests.

features.title: Multi-Role AI Challenger
features.description: A Claude agent separately interrogates Business (perceived value) and IT (estimated effort), generates clarifying questions, and computes a confidence index per declaration.

features.title: Conflict Map
features.description: Visual mapping of the Business/IT perception delta, with a conflict threshold configurable at the deployment level (currently 20 points) to flag projects needing mediation before arbitration.

features.title: Scenarios & Arbitration Cut-Line
features.description: Side-by-side project ranking under two scoring scenarios (MVP / Full) with an adjustable cut-line, plus forced inclusion always justified and logged.

image.alt: Screenshot of the AGAP demo dashboard: a portfolio of 6 fictional projects with their arbitration status, in read-only demonstration mode.

lexguard.title: LexGuard
lexguard.description: Detects red-flag signals in contracts before signature.
lexguard.demonstrates: Making a contract readable for a non-lawyer: red-flag signal detection and a plain-language verdict.
lexguard.challenge: The mayor of a rural town, with no legal department, signs a telecom equipment contract under sales pressure — one that conceals a second leasing agreement with a long commitment term and near-impossible termination. Some towns have been sued for tens of thousands of euros after the fact.
lexguard.solution: A demonstration that analyzes a contract submitted as a PDF and flags, before signature, the warning signs of a risky arrangement (concealed contract, abnormal duration, tacit renewal) — in plain language, without ever ruling on the contract's legality or a company's reliability.

features.title: Red-flag signal detection
features.description: Identifies patterns of risky contractual arrangements.

features.title: Plain-language verdict
features.description: 3-level assessment, no legal jargon.

features.title: No application-side storage
features.description: The document is processed in memory and is not stored by the application. The AI provider (Anthropic) retains transmitted data for 30 days, under its default policy.

image.alt: Screenshot of the LexGuard homepage: contract upload, an example of a detected warning signal, and the guarantee that no uploaded document is stored.

comex.title: Comex
comex.description: Strategic framing and alignment through AI.
comex.demonstrates: Structuring AI framing: from questionnaire to two AI-costed implementation paths.
comex.challenge: Executive committees face a growing volume of AI initiatives without structured tooling to prioritize, frame, and align them with company strategic objectives in a controlled timeframe.
comex.solution: An AI proposal generator powered by Claude: a structured framing questionnaire (19 questions), followed by an AI clarification exchange (up to 4 targeted questions), leading to two implementation proposals — a "quick" one (under 3 months, existing stack) and a "balanced" one (3-6 month MVP) — with budget, timeline and risks estimated by the AI.

features.title: Framing + AI Clarification
features.description: 19 structured questions, followed by an AI clarification exchange (up to 4 targeted questions) to refine the diagnosis.

features.title: Two Costed Proposals
features.description: A "quick" proposal (under 3 months, existing stack) and a "balanced" proposal (3-6 month MVP), with budget, timeline and risks estimated by the AI.

features.title: Tailored to Your Environment
features.description: Proposals take the declared IT stack into account (cloud and AI provider already in place).

sirene.title: Sirene
sirene.demonstrates: Making a public API accessible in natural language, with a lightweight model (Claude Haiku).
sirene.challenge: Sales and operations teams waste valuable time identifying and qualifying companies through the standard INSEE Sirene interface. Rigid filter syntax and lack of semantic understanding hinder adoption.
sirene.solution: An AI assistant that understands natural language queries and interrogates the INSEE Sirene API to return structured and filtered results — with no technical knowledge required from the user.

features.title: Natural Language Queries
features.description: Translation of the query into Sirene API parameters by an LLM (Claude Haiku).

features.title: Sector and Region Filters
features.description: NAF sector and region inferred from free-form expressions, with a filter on administrative status (active or discontinued companies).

features.title: Results Export
features.description: CSV and Excel export of results.

dvf.title: DVF
dvf.description: Real estate transaction search and analysis.
dvf.demonstrates: Using open land-registry data: address search and municipality-level price statistics.
dvf.challenge: Analyzing DVF (Property Value Requests) data published by the DGFiP is tedious: multi-GB raw CSV format, no native visualization, and difficulty cross-referencing with geographic data.
dvf.solution: A search platform for real estate and land transactions, with land price statistics by municipality from DGFiP open data.

features.title: Median Land Price by Municipality
features.description: Median price per m² and land area, with year-by-year evolution, calculated for each municipality from DVF transaction data.

features.title: Address-Based Transaction Search
features.description: Geolocated search for real estate and land sale transactions around an address, with automatic fallback to a wider radius.

verifid.title: ID Document Verifier
verifid.description: AI-powered document quality control and MRZ consistency check.
verifid.demonstrates: Combining AI reading with a deterministic calculation (MRZ check digits) to make verification more reliable.
verifid.challenge: A subscription file with an illegible or incomplete ID gets stuck until a handler notices it and contacts the client — a back-and-forth cycle that degrades completion rates and burdens the back office.
verifid.solution: A demonstration that checks the quality of an identity document at upload time (legibility, completeness, framing) and has the AI read its MRZ, then checks its mathematical consistency against ICAO 9303 — without ever judging its authenticity.

features.title: Instant quality control
features.description: Detection in seconds of blurry photos, glare, or partially out-of-frame documents, before a file ever reaches a handler.

features.title: Verifiable MRZ consistency
features.description: Deterministic ICAO 9303 check-digit calculation (ID card and passport), with the details shown. The characters are read by the AI: the calculation is transparent, the reading can be wrong.

features.title: Front/back cross-check
features.description: Comparison of the document number between both sides of the card, as an additional consistency signal.

metadata.title: AI Method: From Diagnosis to Production | TKoidra
metadata.description: A three-stage AI method — diagnose, build, operate — with guardrails, evaluation and compliance from the start, proven online.
metadata.ogTitle: AI Method: From Diagnosis to Production

methode.title: From Diagnosis to Controlled Production
methode.lead: In my experience, a generative AI project stumbles less on the model than on the move from prototype to production: data, security, costs, compliance, adoption. My method addresses these issues from day one, in three stages. The guides that follow draw on what I actually did on my online demonstrators, using fictional data.
methode.stepperLabel: The three phases of the method

phases.name: Diagnose
phases.goal: Decide quickly and well. Where does AI create value, and is the project worth building?
actions: Start from the mission, not the tool: what business problem, for whom, and how will it be measured?
A real inventory: what actually runs, not what the documentation says — data, information system, security, regulatory constraints.
Use cases grounded in the field: confronting management's vision with the reality of the teams.
Prioritisation by value, feasibility and risk, operating cost included.
A go/no-go decision, with success criteria and an acceptance floor set before writing the first line.

phases.name: Build
phases.goal: Deliver a prototype that runs online, measured, safe and compliant. Not a throwaway demo.
actions: Short batches, each testable and deployable, with a read-only analysis and a validated plan before any change.
Guardrails first: spending caps, quotas, input limits, neutral error messages, secrets kept out of the code, least-privilege accounts.
A model chosen on explicit criteria: quality on the use case, cost, latency, output format, provider compliance.
Answers grounded in sources: mandatory citations, explicit refusal when information is missing.
Evaluation before any deployment: reference question set, edge cases, go/no-go floor, measured cost.
Compliance by design: data retention checked in the providers' official policies, accurate consent, limits displayed.

phases.name: Operate
phases.goal: That the solution holds over time, costs what was planned, and is actually used.
actions: Progressive deployment: the new version is deployed without traffic, tested under real conditions, then switched over. Rollback is ready in one command.
Observability: logs without user content, audit lines, cost tracked for every request.
Incident management: root cause established from the logs before any fix.
Planned maintenance: recurring checks, dependencies, regressions, dated log.
Tracking value and adoption: KPIs compared with the baseline, user feedback, adjustments.

guides.title: Choosing the right use cases
guides.seenSometimes: Each department arrives with its own list of AI ideas, and the committee decides in favor of whichever is argued the loudest. People start from the tool ("we need a chatbot") rather than the problem, and find out too late that the data does not exist or that a simple rule would have been enough.
howTo: **A single entry point, a common scoring grid** for every department: you compare projects, not speakers.
**Start from business pain points**, not solutions: how much time or money is lost today, and what does an error cost?

**Filter before assessing: is it really an AI problem?** A rule, better document filing or off-the-shelf software is often enough. This is the step that saves the most time. And if AI is justified, start with the simplest solution: an existing tool, then a prompt, then a RAG, with specific training (fine-tuning) as a last resort.

**Assess on four axes**, with each department: value (measurable); feasibility, starting with the data (does it exist, is it accessible, up to date, personal?) and the business requirements (volume, acceptable latency, explainability); risk (cost of a wrong answer, fairness of decisions, GDPR and AI Act constraints); total cost, running costs included.
**Prioritize**: a few quick wins and one or two structural bets, each with a business sponsor.
**Deliver a "no" without surprises**: the department took part in the scoring, and leaves with a clear condition for reopening the case.

illustrations.text: Fraud Agent: the risk score is calculated by rules in code; AI only steps in for what the rules cannot read, such as the narrative of a report.
Comex: a 19-question scoping process that leads to two implementation proposals.
AGAP: a portfolio arbitration that brings out the gap in perception between the business and IT, with scenarios and a cut-off line.

guides.title: From POC to production
guides.seenSometimes: A POC that shines in the demo, then months spent "moving it to production" with no stopping criterion. Nobody measured the starting point: six months later, there is no way to tell whether the project delivered anything.
howTo: **Tell a POC from an MVP.** A proof of concept (POC) proves it can be done, quickly and cheaply: it decides whether the project enters the portfolio. A minimum viable product (MVP) proves it gets used: it decides whether to scale up.
**Set the go/no-go before the test**: a floor (what absolutely has to work) and success criteria, written down before seeing the results.
**Measure the baseline before launch**, with a method (for example a sample of timed searches), and set a target with the business.
**Deliver in short, deployable increments**, guardrails before features.
**Track two control indicators** on top of value: adoption and answer quality.
**Allow yourself to stop**: a regular review where stopping is a real option.
checklist: review with the right to stop

illustrations.text: AssurConseil RAG: the audit of the demo already online first revealed a gap with the documentation, an unconfirmed spending cap and a public secondary instance, so the first increment focused on guardrails, before any feature. Then, two engines evaluated on 20 questions for $0.39, with a floor set before the test; the interface was only built after the green light.

guides.title: Building a reliable RAG
guides.seenSometimes: An assistant plugged into a folder of documents, tested "by eye" on three questions, with a model picked for its reputation. It always answers, even when the information does not exist. Nobody can tell whether it got better or worse after an update.
howTo: **Check that it is a RAG problem**: answering questions from a specific corpus, with a verifiable source. If a standard search is enough, there is no need for AI.

**Qualify the corpus first**: who maintains it, which version is authoritative, does it contain personal data, and what is its quality (completeness, accuracy, timeliness, consistency)? An outdated document or a reference to a non-existent article will produce an answer that is wrong, but well phrased.
**Split along the structure of the documents** (articles, sections) rather than into fixed-size chunks, keeping the references (document, version, article): that is what makes citing possible.
**Measure retrieval separately from the answer.** If the right passage is not retrieved, even the best model cannot answer correctly. Changing the embedding model means re-indexing the whole corpus.
**Constrain the answer**: only from the excerpts, with the source cited, and a **refusal** when the information is missing, tested with out-of-corpus questions.
**Evaluate before delivering** on a question set validated by the business, with thresholds set before the test (see "Evaluating an LLM").
**Secure and cap**: keys kept server-side, quotas and caps, users informed that their data is being sent.
**Re-evaluate after every change** of model, prompt or documents: a RAG can regress without anyone noticing.

illustrations.text: AssurConseil RAG: fictional corpus split by article, cited answers, refusal tested on an out-of-corpus question, two engines compared on the same question set. Known limitation: my automated citation check turned out to be too lenient; I am redoing it with an LLM judge, currently being calibrated.

guides.title: Keeping an AI agent under control
guides.seenSometimes: An agent given powerful tools and instructions in its prompt: "never approve a suspicious claim". The day a document contains a hidden instruction, or the model gets it wrong, nothing stops it from acting.
howTo: **The AI proposes, the code decides.** Decisions that commit the organization (status, amount, routing) are made or checked by deterministic code, not by the model.
**A prompt asks, a schema prevents.** What must not happen is not among the agent's tools: an action missing from its schema is impossible, whatever the prompt says.
**Treat all external content as data**, never as an instruction: a prompt injection comes in through the document, not through the user.
**Recalculate server-side** everything the agent produces that has consequences (amounts, thresholds, inconsistent statuses).
**A human approves** decisions that affect a person, with a mandatory reason for any rejection.
**Check the quota before any external call**: otherwise you pay, and send data, for a result that goes unused.
**Test attacks**, not just the happy path: injections, inconsistent documents, malformed inputs.
checklist: forbidden actions absent from the schema

illustrations.text: Fraud Agent: the agent proposes, a claims handler approves; it cannot change a claim's routing, since it has no field to do so; the triage component can only escalate an alert, never downgrade it; an injection test was carried out. Demonstrator on fictional claims.

guides.title: Evaluating an LLM: reference set and LLM-as-a-judge
guides.seenSometimes: "We tested it, it works." A few questions picked by the team, a flattering average score, and a threshold decided after seeing the results. The day an answer invents a contract condition, nobody understands how it got through the tests.
howTo: **A reference question set (golden set) validated by the business**, representative of real questions, trick and out-of-scope cases included.
**Thresholds set before the test**, never after.

**Blocking criteria, not just an average.** An answer that invents coverage and a clumsy answer weigh the same in an average score: a single failure on a blocking criterion (a claim missing from the sources, a wrong source, no refusal) must block the release.
**Check in code whatever can be checked** (expected citation, format): it is free and reproducible.

**Leave to the LLM judge only what code cannot check**, such as faithfulness to the sources. The judge is itself an LLM, with known biases (a preference for longer answers, or for answers from its own model).

**Calibrate the judge before relying on it**: compare it with blind human scoring, feed it deliberately wrong answers, and set before the test how many traps it must catch and how many disagreements are tolerated. Choose a judge from a different provider than the model being evaluated.
**Freeze the baseline before changing tools**: measure the old system before retiring it, so you can say "it is better", not just "it works".
**Re-evaluate after every change** of model, prompt or documents.
checklist: golden set validated by the business
thresholds written down before the test

illustrations.text: AssurConseil RAG: floor set before the test, out-of-corpus question evaluated separately so that a good average cannot hide it, score of the old search engine frozen before it was retired. In progress: calibration of an LLM judge from another provider, with trap answers, blind human scoring and thresholds set before the test. Known limitation: the human reference is scored by a single person.

guides.title: Choosing a model and keeping costs under control
guides.seenSometimes: The "most powerful model on the market" by default, a bill discovered at the end of the month, and quotas set on average usage. Then one day the provider retires the model, and the application goes down.
howTo: **Put a figure on it before choosing**: cost per question, expected volume, monthly order of magnitude, to be validated with the business.

**Define quality on your own questions**, not on a market leaderboard, then **pick the cheapest model that clears the threshold**. If a requirement (for example exact citation) is critical, it is part of the threshold, and you pay for it.

**Cap costs at three levels**: by design (only call the model when it is useful, cap answer length); through quotas calculated on the **worst case**, not the average; through a spending cap at the provider, dedicated to the project.
**Isolate each project** (dedicated workspace and key) to see its real cost and limit the damage of a compromised key.
**Track model lifecycles**: providers retire models on fixed dates. A migration is tested on the most demanding path, not just the happy path.
**Keep it reversible**: an architecture that lets you compare another provider on the same question set.
checklist: quality threshold defined on your questions
cheapest model that clears the threshold
quotas based on the worst case

illustrations.text: AssurConseil RAG: a model roughly nine times cheaper clears the same floor as Claude, which remains the main engine; Comex: quotas calculated on the worst-case cost of a generation, dedicated spending cap; a migration forced by a model's retirement broke a path my tests did not cover, hence the rule of testing the heaviest path before every migration.

guides.title: Protecting data
guides.seenSometimes: Customer data sent as is to a model provider, without knowing how long it keeps it or whether it uses it to train its models. The DPO finds out about the project a week before go-live.
howTo: **Involve the DPO and the CISO from the scoping stage**, not at the end: data protection impact assessment (DPIA) and AI Act classification before the first increment.
**Send only what is necessary** (data minimization), pseudonymized where possible.
**Inform people** that AI is involved, and of what is sent, before sending it.
**Read the provider's terms**: retention period, use for training (to be refused), data processing agreement; negotiate zero retention when the stakes justify it.
**Know where inference runs**: a European endpoint is no guarantee that all data stays in Europe; you have to read what the provider commits to.
**Clarify the shared responsibility with the provider**: what it guarantees, and what remains your responsibility.
**Keys kept server-side, role-based access, logs without sensitive content**, and any decision affecting a person always signed off by a human.
checklist: DPO and CISO involved from scoping

illustrations.text: my demonstrators: fictional data only (I refused to send real claims to Fraud Agent); information displayed before sending (AI used, retention by the provider); training refused; Mistral inference through the European endpoint.

guides.title: Getting a GenAI application signed off
guides.seenSometimes: The project team presents its own results, the risk function can only read them, and sign-off rests on trust. The file says what works, rarely what does not.
howTo: **Clarify who signs**, according to the organization's governance: usually the business owner, after input from the risk, compliance, security and DPO functions.
**Meet the risk function at the start**, to learn what a file must contain, rather than finding out at sign-off.

**A file built to be challenged**: intended and prohibited uses, data sent and to whom, evaluation protocol with thresholds set beforehand, **all** results, bad ones included, known limitations, guardrails, monitoring plan.
**Make everything replayable**: question set, scoring grid and scripts, so that the risk function can rerun the tests itself. A validation that can only read is not independent.
**One common framework for all applications**, tested on a pilot first, rather than a different file for each project.
checklist: risk function met at the start

illustrations.text: AssurConseil RAG: a public "Choix et limites" (choices and limitations) page documents the model used, the data sent, the guardrails, and what the evaluation does and does not measure.

guides.title: Shipping without breaking things
guides.seenSometimes: A change pushed straight to production "because it's small", an "all tests pass" report accepted without checking, and blind faith in the rollback button.
howTo: **Prove it on a copy of production**: every pull request creates a preview, tested by a person on the real user journey. Something missing (a file that should not be public) does not show up in a code review, only in testing.
**Make the differences between environments deliberate and listed** (quotas, keys, services): an unintended difference sends a never-tested feature to production.
**Take no report at face value**, whether it comes from a developer or a coding agent: demand the raw test output, step by step.
**Run tests automatically** (continuous integration) and make their status a merge blocker.
**Check in production after merging**: a successful deployment does not prove that the user journey works.
**Know what a rollback does not undo**: data already exposed, a secret already leaked, a database already migrated.
checklist: a preview for each pull request
human test of the user journey

illustrations.text: my demonstrators: one branch and one pull request per increment, merged by me after testing in preview, then checked in production; it was the preview test, not the code review, that revealed a configuration flaw before production. Known limitation: my tests do not run in continuous integration yet.

guides.title: Monitoring and handling incidents
guides.seenSometimes: Outages are reported by users, answer quality is no longer measured once in production, and every incident ends with "it's fixed", with nothing to stop it from happening again.
howTo: **Detect before the user does**: a probe that replays the main user journey at regular intervals, alerts on server errors and on spending; monitor latency, traffic, saturation and errors, and set service level objectives (SLOs) on the ones that matter to the user. Without this, an outage lasts until someone notices it.
**Beware of what breaks nothing**: a data exposure or an authorization flaw triggers no alert, and lasts as long as nobody looks for it.
**Contain**: measure the impact (who, which data), roll back to the previous version, inform the people affected and the sponsor (what we know, what we are doing, when we will next update).
**Fix once things are calm**: look for the root cause in the logs once production is stable.
**Learn without blame**: distinguish the immediate cause from the root cause, and produce a rule or a tool.
**Plan for recovery**: backups and a recovery plan that are tested, not just written down; regulatory and security watch.

**Monitor answer quality too**: a report button whose every confirmed case joins the test set, and a random sample of production answers scored with the same grid, because reports only catch the errors someone notices. Keeping real answers is a trade-off to settle with the DPO.
checklist: probe on the main user journey
reports linked to the test set

illustrations.text: my demonstrators, known limitation: they do not have automated monitoring yet. An outage after a key change was spotted through testing, not by an alert; it led to a rule (add the new key, redeploy, test in production, and only then revoke the old one). This guide describes what I would put in place on a real project.

guides.title: Driving AI adoption
guides.seenSometimes: A tool delivered that works, a one-hour training session, a newsletter, and three months later hardly anyone uses it. Adoption was thought about after delivery.
howTo: **Start from the mission, not the tool**: AI addresses a pain point the teams recognize.
**Involve future users from the scoping stage**, not just at acceptance testing.
**Measure usage and perceived quality**, alongside value: low adoption is a signal to understand, not to hide.
**Remove the concrete obstacles**: trust in the answers (visible sources), the tool's place in the workflow, clear rules on what can be put into it.
**A visible sponsor and champions within the teams.**
checklist: pain point recognized by the teams

illustrations.text: my fifteen-year background in change management, agile facilitation and Product Ownership. No illustration on my demonstrators yet, as they have no user population to bring on board.

operatingMode.title: My operating mode: AI accelerates, humans decide

steps.title: Plan and get it approved
steps.text: No change without an approved plan.

steps.title: Deliver in small batches
steps.text: One commit per topic, automated tests, a reviewed preview.

steps.title: Keep control of production
steps.text: Any command that touches it is run by a human, after verification.

operatingMode.quote: I develop with AI coding agents under this protocol. It is what makes it possible to move fast without losing control, and it is the same discipline I bring to your teams.

cta.text: Framing an AI project, or looking for someone to take it all the way to production? Let's talk.
